title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
hook: he turns toward Jerusalem, and the foxes have holes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve sent out with nothing, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was nothing for the journey. What did you leave behind? Day four hundred fifty-nine.

Partway through Luke's Gospel, the book turns. Until now Jesus has been moving around Galilee: the lake, the villages, the hills. Then, in one verse, he turns toward Jerusalem. From here on, Luke tells the story as one long walk to the city where, as Jesus has already told his disciples, he will suffer. Readers call this stretch the travel narrative. And the very first thing that happens on the road is a door shut in his face. Today, the turn.
screen: `IN ONE VERSE, THE BOOK TURNS.` → `ONE LONG WALK TO JERUSALEM.` → `A DOOR SHUTS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the hinge in the Douay-Rheims: "And it came to pass, when the days of his assumption were accomplishing, that he steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." Assumption here means his being taken up, to the cross and to the Father. To set your face is an old Hebrew way of speaking: to fix your direction and refuse to be turned. Isaiah's servant says he has set his face hard as rock. Jesus sends messengers ahead into a Samaritan village, and the village won't receive him, because he's headed for Jerusalem. James and John ask if they should call fire down from heaven. Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they simply go on to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you wherever you go. Jesus answers: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Know what you're signing up for. The second says, let me first go and bury my father. The third says, let me first say goodbye at home. And Jesus answers with a farmer's picture: "No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." Anyone who has plowed knows why. If you look over your shoulder, the furrow wanders. These sayings are hard, and Luke doesn't soften them. The Church reads them not as contempt for family, which the commandments honor, but as a question of what comes first. Jesus has set his face. He asks the people walking beside him to set theirs.
screen: `THE DAYS OF HIS ASSUMPTION.` · `NO FIRE ON THE SAMARITAN VILLAGE.` · `THE FOXES HAVE HOLES.` · `A HAND ON THE PLOW.` · then, large: `HE STEADFASTLY SET HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: commit to one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been circling: a conversation you keep postponing, a habit you keep almost starting, a decision you keep reopening. Pick one. Now picture yourself setting your face toward it, the way you'd turn to walk a road. What's the first step, today? Name it. Notice the urge to look back, the reasons to wait. Let them be there, and keep facing forward. If you pray, ask for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
assumption. Luke's word for Jesus being taken up, to the cross and to the Father, the hinge where he fixed his face toward Jerusalem. Today's word.
Your line: no looking back. Today, take the first step on your one hard thing, and when you want to turn around, keep your hand on the plow. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this passage at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel; the Catechism teaches that family ties matter but are not absolute, and that following Jesus comes first.

fork.setup: you're James. a Samaritan village has refused to welcome your teacher. what do you suggest?
options: call down fire from heaven on them.
fork.reveal: James and John offer fire. Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they simply go on to another village.

trapdoor: what you thought: he set his face means he looked determined.
what it means: it's a Hebrew idiom for fixing your direction and refusing to turn, and here it means toward the cross.
what a scholar hears: the journey to Jerusalem begins at 9:51; the phrase echoes Isaiah 50:7, where the servant sets his face like hard rock.
